title: Home & everyday objects
goal: Describe a home, say where things are (in, on, under, near…), and say what there is and what you have.
intro:
Where are my keys? Is there a fan in the room? Do you have a pen? In this unit you'll learn rooms, furniture and household objects, and the **postpositions** that say where things are.

Hindi has *post*positions, not prepositions: they come **after** the noun — मेज़ **पर** 'on the table', literally 'table on'. You'll also learn the small spelling change nouns go through before a postposition (the 'oblique case').

m · pl: कमरे · oblique: कमरे में
f · also रसोईघर, and 'किचन' in cities
m · पंखा चलाना 'to switch on the fan'
f · flat roofs are used for drying clothes, flying kites, sleeping in summer
के पास 'near X'; मेरे पास 'with me' = I have

phrases.en: The books are in the cupboard.
How many rooms are there in the house?

phrases.native: रसोई के बगल में बाथरूम है।
phrases.roman: rasoī ke bagal meṃ bāthrūm hai.
phrases.en: There's a bathroom next to the kitchen.

grammar.title: Postpositions and the oblique case
grammar.body:
Hindi puts **में** 'in', **पर** 'on', **से** 'from', **को** 'to', **तक** 'up to' **after** the noun: मेज़ पर 'on the table'.

Longer 'compound' postpositions are made with **के**: **के ऊपर** 'above', **के नीचे** 'under', **के पास** 'near', **के अंदर** 'inside', **के बाहर** 'outside', **के पीछे** 'behind', **के सामने** 'opposite', **के बगल में** 'next to': मेज़ के नीचे 'under the table'.

Before any postposition, nouns take the **oblique** form:

**m. ending in -ā** → -e: कमरा → कमरे में, दरवाज़ा → दरवाज़े के पास
**all plurals** → -oṃ: कमरों में, किताबों पर, लड़कियों के लिए
Other singular nouns don't change: घर में, मेज़ पर, खिड़की के पास.

Pronouns also change: मैं → **मेरे** पास, वह → **उसके** पीछे, यह → **इसमें** 'in this'.

examples.native: घर के सामने एक पेड़ है।
examples.roman: ghar ke sāmne ek peṛ hai.
examples.en: There's a tree in front of the house.
The cat is on top of the bed.

grammar.title: 'There is / there are' and 'I have'
grammar.body:
Hindi doesn't need a special word for 'there is': just say the place first, then the thing, then **है** (one) or **हैं** (several): **कमरे में एक पंखा है** 'There's a fan in the room' (lit. 'in the room a fan is').

For 'there isn't', put नहीं before the verb (or drop the verb): कमरे में पंखा नहीं है.

For **possessing** objects (things you could hand over), Hindi says 'near me there is': **मेरे पास** एक गाड़ी है 'I have a car'. (For relatives and body parts you use मेरे / मेरी … है, as in Unit 3.)

examples.en: There's a fridge in the kitchen.
There are two photos on the wall.
There's no light in the bathroom.

dialogue.title: Looking at a flat
dialogue.setting: Daniel is looking at a flat to rent. The landlord, Mr Gupta, shows him around.

lines.speaker: Mr Gupta
lines.native: आइए, अंदर आइए। यह बैठक है।
lines.roman: āiye, andar āiye. yah baiṭhak hai.
lines.en: Come, come in. This is the living room.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.native: अच्छा है। घर में कितने कमरे हैं?
lines.roman: achchhā hai. ghar meṃ kitne kamre haiṃ?
lines.en: It's nice. How many rooms are there in the flat?

lines.speaker: Mr Gupta
lines.native: दो कमरे, एक रसोई और एक बाथरूम।
lines.roman: do kamre, ek rasoī aur ek bāthrūm.
lines.en: Two rooms, a kitchen and a bathroom.

lines.speaker: Mr Gupta
lines.native: वहाँ, बाथरूम के बगल में। रसोई में फ़्रिज भी है।
lines.roman: vahāṃ, bāthrūm ke bagal meṃ. rasoī meṃ frij bhī hai.
lines.en: Over there, next to the bathroom. There's a fridge in the kitchen too.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.en: And are there fans in the rooms?

lines.speaker: Mr Gupta
lines.native: जी हाँ, हर कमरे में पंखा और अलमारी है।
lines.roman: jī hāṃ, har kamre meṃ paṅkhā aur almārī hai.
lines.en: Yes, every room has a fan and a wardrobe.

lines.speaker: Mr Gupta
lines.native: सीढ़ियाँ दरवाज़े के पीछे हैं। ऊपर छत पर बहुत अच्छी हवा है।
lines.roman: sīṛhiyāṃ darvāze ke pīchhe haiṃ. ūpar chhat par bahut achchhī havā hai.
lines.en: The stairs are behind the door. Up on the roof there's a lovely breeze.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.native: ठीक है, मुझे घर पसंद है!
lines.roman: ṭhīk hai, mujhe ghar pasand hai!

culture: Shoes usually come off at the door of an Indian home, and often before entering the kitchen or a prayer area. Many homes have a small shrine (पूजा का कमरा or a corner shelf). In much of India the flat roof (छत) is living space — for drying clothes and chillies, flying kites on festivals, and sleeping on hot summer nights. Note that घर means both 'house' and 'home', and Indians say घर पर 'at home' or simply घर: मैं घर जा रहा हूँ 'I'm going home'.
